title: How Rehab Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of rehab, starting with 19th-century sober houses and the temperance movement, through prohibition, the 1935 founding of Alcoholics Anonymous, Nixon and Ford drug policy and the Betty Ford Clinic, and the shift to the brain disease model of addiction in the 1980s. They cover treatment types (inpatient, outpatient, methadone treatment, partial hospitalization, prison rehab), how rehab works (detox, twelve-step programs, cognitive behavioral counseling, medication, alternative methods like acupuncture and Narconon-style programs), success and relapse studies, costs and celebrity luxury rehab centers, insurance and taxpayer burden, and cost-benefit figures. The episode closes with a listener mail about a 12-year-old fan raising money for Kiva and a plug for James Frey's A Million Little Pieces.

segments.title: Opening banter and Walter Matthau
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about actor Walter Matthau and his drinking in Bad News Bears, framing rehab as the third topic in an addiction trilogy after addiction and prohibition.

segments.title: Early rehab history and the rise of rehab in the 1980s
segments.summary: Before the 1980s, alcoholics were sent to sanitariums, asylums or medical hospitals. Rehab as known today began in the eighties. Mention of Valley of the Dolls and early treatment practices such as shock treatment and lobotomy.

segments.title: Addiction as a brain disease
segments.summary: The hosts trace how views of addiction shifted from blaming the substance, to seeing it as a character flaw in the 19th century, to the brain disease model that emerged in the 1980s, in which the reward center is hijacked and relapse is expected.

segments.title: Temperance movement, sober houses and prohibition
segments.summary: Temperance and prohibition led to sober houses, which were early rehab-like centers where drinkers were sequestered from alcohol. Prohibition reduced overall drinking but the number of alcoholics reportedly increased.

segments.title: Alcoholics Anonymous and the Betty Ford Clinic
segments.summary: Alcoholics Anonymous was founded in 1935 by Bill Wilson and Dr. Bob, drawing on earlier temperance-era support groups such as the International Order of Good Templars. Under Nixon and Ford, drug policy shifted toward treatment, and Betty Ford opened the Betty Ford Clinic in Rancho Mirage, California, in 1982, which helped reduce stigma. Under Reagan the war on drugs continued and private rehab institutions boomed.

segments.title: Types of treatment: inpatient, outpatient, methadone and partial hospitalization
segments.summary: Overview of treatment formats. Inpatient means residing at the facility, often 28 days, sometimes longer or court-ordered. Outpatient involves regular visits while living at home. Methadone treatment is usually outpatient. Partial hospitalization means spending the full day in treatment while sleeping at home. Prison-based rehab is also discussed.

segments.title: How rehab works: detox, twelve steps, counseling and medication
segments.summary: Rehab starts with withdrawal and detox, followed by twelve-step programs. Discussion of AA's success and criticism, its God-based framing ('God as you understand him'), and Narcotics Anonymous's adaptation for atheists. Cognitive behavioral counseling is described, with studies showing it is less effective than twelve-step programs. Medication such as methadone is used when needed, and treating co-occurring conditions together is effective.

segments.title: Alternative treatments and luxury rehab options
segments.summary: Acupuncture is discussed as a non-traditional method the hosts have tried. Scientology's Narconon-style program is mentioned as a no-medication approach. Higher-end programs offer extras such as helicopter rides and wilderness survival.

segments.title: Success rates, relapse studies and readiness to change
segments.summary: A study cited an 87 percent chance of not relapsing after six months when combining inpatient treatment, twelve-step groups and counseling. Twelve-step attendance proved most significant, followed by individual counseling. Success depends on the person being ready to change. Forced rehab in prison also showed reasonably high abstinence and lower recidivism. Drug courts refer offenders to treatment.

segments.title: Statistics, costs, celebrity rehab and taxpayer burden
segments.summary: About 3.9 million people entered treatment around 2005 and 2008 figures were similar; roughly 1.3 million were treated for both drugs and alcohol. Average costs in 2002 were about $400 for residential... Costs of luxury centers such as Promises, Crossroads (Antigua, founded by Eric Clapton) and Sanctuary (Byron Bay, Australia) are discussed. Insurance and Medicaid shifted costs to the state; a study found every dollar spent on rehab returned about three dollars in reduced societal cost. Estimated 12 million alcoholics affect many more people.

segments.title: Sponsor and site promotion
segments.summary: Brief promotion for the How Stuff Works website, its articles and an upcoming app.

segments.title: Listener mail: twelve-year-old Emma and Kiva
segments.summary: A listener mail from twelve-year-old Emma, who plans to walk dogs and babysit to raise money to donate to Kiva.

segments.title: Sign-off and book mention
segments.summary: Hosts mention James Frey's A Million Little Pieces, a memoir later found to be untrue, and close the episode.
